body:
From ordinary light to quantum information

Communication means transferring information from a sender to a receiver. In an ordinary digital network, information is represented by bits, each having the value 0 or 1. Electrical signals, radio waves or pulses of light can carry these bits. Optical-fibre networks guide light through a transparent fibre, while free-space optical links send light through the air.

Light has both wave-like and particle-like properties. Its smallest packets of energy are called photons. At the school level, reflection and refraction explain how light changes direction; quantum physics explains how individual photons can be prepared and measured in different states. A qubit, or quantum bit, is a unit of quantum information. Unlike a classical bit, a qubit can exist in a superposition of possible states, although an individual measurement produces a definite outcome. This does not allow a receiver to read 0 and 1 simultaneously.

One property used in quantum communication is polarisation, which describes the orientation of light's electric-field oscillation. Different photon polarisations can be chosen to represent information. Another way of encoding information uses distinct times at which light pulses arrive. The important point is not the particular method, but that the information is carried in quantum states.

Why quantum states help reveal interception

In ordinary communication, an interceptor may copy a transmitted digital signal without necessarily changing the original bits. Quantum information behaves differently. An unknown quantum state cannot, in general, be copied perfectly; this is called the no-cloning principle. Moreover, measuring a photon in an unsuitable way can disturb the state that the legitimate receiver would subsequently measure.

In quantum key distribution (QKD), these properties allow the sender and receiver to test statistically whether their exchange may have been disturbed. A disturbance can indicate eavesdropping, although equipment imperfections and ordinary transmission noise can also produce errors. Detection is therefore not guaranteed from one intercepted photon; security depends on testing the exchange and using an appropriate protocol.

Quantum communication uses quantum states to transmit or share information. QKD is a particular application used to establish a secret encryption key between legitimate users.

Prelims focus

  • A classical bit has the value 0 or 1; a qubit is quantum information.
  • A photon is a quantum of light; photon polarisation can carry quantum information.
  • QKD uses quantum-state properties to help detect interception of a key exchange.
  • Trap: QKD does not mean that every transmitted message is itself a quantum signal.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, ch. 11, Light, Shadows and Reflections, printed pp. 107–113; NCERT, Science, Class 8, ch. 16, Light, printed pp. 199–201; NCERT, Science, Class 10, ch. 9, Light – Reflection and Refraction, printed p. 134; NIST, What Is Quantum Cryptography?, sections on quantum principles and photon measurements (accessed 5 November 2026).]

title: Quantum Communication: The Basic Scientific Ideas

body:
Why a shared encryption key is necessary

A secret message can be protected by an encryption key, a sequence of bits used by an encryption system to turn readable information into unreadable ciphertext and recover it later. If 2 users use a shared-key encryption system, both must possess the correct secret key. Transmitting that key insecurely would defeat the purpose of encryption.

QKD addresses the key-sharing problem. It does not by itself encrypt a document, a video call or a bank transaction. Instead, it helps legitimate users establish matching secret key material, which can then be used by an ordinary encryption system to protect the actual data.

The basic steps of QKD

The conventional names in explanations are Alice for the sender, Bob for the receiver and Eve for a possible eavesdropper. A well-known introductory method is BB84, proposed by Charles H. Bennett and Gilles Brassard in 1984.

  1. Prepare and send: Alice makes random choices and prepares photon states to represent possible key bits. In a simple explanation of BB84, she also varies the basis, or set of polarisation directions, used to prepare them.
  2. Measure: Bob measures the received photons, choosing measurement bases without knowing all Alice's choices. A compatible choice allows him to recover the intended bit reliably in an ideal, undisturbed transmission; an incompatible choice does not.
  3. Compare suitable information publicly: Alice and Bob use an authenticated classical channel, which lets each user verify that the other's messages are genuine and unaltered, to compare which bases they used, without revealing the secret bit values. They keep results associated with compatible bases and discard the rest.
  4. Check errors and protect secrecy: They compare selected results to estimate disturbances and discard these publicly revealed bits, then use error correction to reconcile the remaining bits and privacy amplification to produce a shorter key about which an interceptor has negligible information. If the error level is unacceptable, they do not use that exchange as a secure key.
  5. Encrypt the message: After establishing a suitable shared key, they can encrypt and transmit the message through a conventional communication channel.

What an eavesdropper changes

If Eve intercepts and measures photons without knowing how Alice prepared them, some of her measurement choices may be incompatible. The states she forwards can then cause additional errors in Bob's results. By testing a suitable portion of the exchange, Alice and Bob can estimate whether it is safe to continue. The test does not reveal Eve's identity, and a raised error rate alone does not prove that an attacker was present.

QKD can use entanglement, but need not

BB84 is an example of prepare-and-measure QKD: Alice prepares states and Bob measures them. In entanglement-based QKD, users make use of specially correlated pairs of quantum particles. When measured in suitable ways, the particles show related outcomes that can help the users establish and test key material.

Entanglement is a distinctive quantum correlation; it does not permit faster-than-light messaging. Neither entanglement nor a quantum computer is required for every QKD system. This distinction explains why Indian reports separately describe prepare-and-measure demonstrations and entanglement-based demonstrations.

QKD involves a quantum channel for key establishment and an authenticated classical channel for coordination. The eventual encrypted data can travel through ordinary networks.

Prelims focus

  • QKD stands for Quantum Key Distribution.
  • BB84 was introduced by Bennett and Brassard in 1984.
  • Matching preparation and measurement bases are important in the simple BB84 explanation.
  • Eavesdropping may increase detectable errors in quantum measurements.
  • Trap: Entanglement is useful in some QKD methods, but QKD does not always require entangled particles.

[Sources: IBM Quantum Learning, Quantum Key Distribution, introductory protocol and Caveats sections (accessed 5 November 2026); IBM Newsroom, IBM Fellow and Quantum Pioneer Charles H. Bennett Receives A.M. Turing Award, 18 March 2026; NIST, What Is Quantum Cryptography?, sections on photons, eavesdropping and system limitations (accessed 5 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: The quantum exchange establishes a key; an ordinary channel carries the encrypted message.

pictures.alt: Prepare-and-measure QKD sends Alice's prepared photons to Bob; entanglement-based QKD distributes correlated pairs. Both aim to establish and test a secret key.

title: Quantum Key Distribution: How a Secret Key Is Shared

body:
How quantum signals reach another user

A quantum-secure link is a connection designed to protect communication using quantum-security methods, often QKD-generated keys together with ordinary data encryption. The physical route matters because quantum signals are sensitive to loss and disturbance. Three important settings are optical fibre, free space and proposed or developing satellite-based links.

Link typeHow the quantum signal travelsImportant distinction
Optical-fibre QKDLight travels through fibre between stations.Suitable for existing ground telecom corridors; losses limit direct distances.
Free-space QKDLight travels through air across a line-of-sight path.No connecting fibre is needed, but alignment and atmospheric conditions matter.
Satellite-based quantum linksOptical quantum signals may connect satellites and ground stations.Offer a route toward long-distance links; a national target is not proof of an operational satellite service.

A long network is not necessarily one uninterrupted quantum link. In some practical QKD networks, trusted nodes connect shorter sections. Such intermediate sites must remain secure because they take part in handling key material. The quantum no-cloning principle also prevents simply copying an unknown photon state as one might amplify an ordinary digital signal.

Distinguishing QKD, PQC and QRNG

Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is different from quantum communication. PQC uses mathematical algorithms intended to resist attacks by powerful quantum computers; it can run on conventional computing and communications systems without carrying photon states between sites.

Quantum random number generation (QRNG) uses unpredictable quantum events as a source of random numbers. High-quality random numbers can help generate cryptographic keys, but a QRNG by itself does not distribute a shared key between distant users.

These approaches can complement one another. For example, a service may use QKD to obtain key material, PQC for additional cryptographic protection, and a QRNG for randomness. The presence of one does not imply the presence of the others.

Applications and the meaning of security

Secure key sharing may be valuable for defence communications, government networks, banks, and protection of other sensitive digital information. QKD offers a way to reveal certain forms of interception of quantum signals, but it is not a guarantee that the entire network is impossible to hack. Faulty equipment, compromised endpoints, insecure authentication, weak implementation or attacks on the ordinary encryption system remain possible.

The classical messages used to coordinate QKD must be authenticated so that Alice knows she is communicating with Bob rather than an impersonator. A secure quantum link also needs workable equipment and sufficiently low transmission errors. For these reasons, a reported laboratory demonstration, a product announcement, an operational service and an announced national goal are different kinds of achievement.

Prelims focus

  • Fibre QKD uses optical fibre; free-space QKD uses a line-of-sight optical path.
  • QKD establishes secret key material; PQC protects communication using quantum-resistant mathematical algorithms.
  • QRNG generates random numbers and is not the same as QKD.
  • Long-distance networks may include trusted intermediate nodes.
  • Trap: A QKD link does not automatically secure compromised computers or authenticate the sender.

[Sources: NIST, What Is Quantum Cryptography?, sections on practical limitations; NIST, What Is Post-Quantum Cryptography?, comparison with quantum cryptography; US National Security Agency, Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and Quantum Cryptography (QC), Technical Limitations section (all accessed 5 November 2026); ISRO, Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), free-space demonstration description (accessed 5 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Two fibre QKD segments meet at a trusted node that handles key material and must be secured; unknown quantum states cannot simply be copied.
pictures.caption: A multi-section QKD network may require trusted intermediate nodes.

title: Quantum-Secure Links: Transmission Methods, Uses and Limits

body:
The first defence and space demonstrations

9 December 2020: The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) reported successful trials of quantum key distribution between 2 of its Hyderabad laboratories: the Defence Research and Development Laboratory (DRDL) and Research Centre Imarat (RCI). The QKD technology was developed by DRDO units including CAIR, Bengaluru, and DYSL-QT, Mumbai. This was an indigenous defence-sector demonstration of secure key exchange, not the announcement of a nationwide QKD network.

19 March 2021: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) demonstrated free-space quantum-secure communication across 300 m between buildings at its Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad. The method was prepare-and-measure QKD, and quantum-key-protected videoconferencing was shown. The photons travelled through air between buildings; the demonstration was not a satellite-to-ground link.

Telecom development and the next Ahmedabad milestone

October 2021: The Centre for Development of Telematics (C-DOT), the Indian telecom research organisation under the Department of Telecommunications, inaugurated a quantum communication laboratory in Delhi and unveiled an indigenous QKD solution described as capable of operating over more than 100 km of standard optical fibre. A product's stated supported distance should not be confused with an independently described outdoor field link.

27 January 2022: Scientists from SAC and the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), both in Ahmedabad, demonstrated entanglement-based QKD across a 300 m free-space path. They also showed quantum-key-secured text, images and 2-way video communication. This experiment and the 2021 demonstration used the same stated distance but different quantum approaches: prepare-and-measure in 2021 and entanglement-based in 2022.

A field demonstration between 2 Uttar Pradesh cities

23 February 2022: A joint DRDO and IIT Delhi team reported a QKD link of more than 100 km between Prayagraj and Vindhyachal, Uttar Pradesh, over commercially available optical fibre. This is a distinct milestone from the Ahmedabad free-space experiments: it used a long existing fibre route rather than an atmospheric link between nearby buildings.

Distance alone does not identify a QKD milestone. Always match the date, institutions, place and type of link. In particular, the 2021 and 2022 Ahmedabad demonstrations were ground-based, although they supported research toward future satellite-based quantum communication.

Prelims focus

  • 2020: DRDO, DRDL–RCI, Hyderabad.
  • 2021: ISRO SAC, Ahmedabad, 300 m free-space prepare-and-measure QKD.
  • 2021: C-DOT unveiled an indigenous fibre-QKD system described as supporting more than 100 km.
  • 2022: SAC and PRL, Ahmedabad, 300 m entanglement-based QKD.
  • 2022: DRDO and IIT Delhi, Prayagraj–Vindhyachal, more than 100 km over optical fibre.

[Sources: Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, Quantum Communication between two DRDO Laboratories, 9 December 2020; ISRO, Department of Space Demonstrates Entanglement Based Quantum Communication over 300m Free Space, 27 January 2022, including its 19 March 2021 milestone; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Communications, Secretary Telecom Visits C-DOT; Inaugurates Futuristic Quantum Communication Lab, 10 October 2021; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Defence, DRDO and IIT Delhi Scientists Demonstrate Quantum Key Distribution between Two Cities 100 Kilometres Apart, 23 February 2022 (online sources accessed 5 November 2026).]
